prompt: For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally and has no pulse, rescuers should

options.text: Begin high-quality CPR and use an AED as soon as available
Call for help and wait for EMS before starting compressions
Start with 2 rescue breaths, then begin compressions at 30:2
Check a pulse for up to 30 seconds before starting compressions

explanation: Adult cardiac arrest care prioritizes immediate compressions (starting CPR with chest compressions) and early defibrillation.

distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for EMS delays compressions; every minute without CPR lowers the chance of survival.
distractorExplanations.c: Breaths-first (A-B-C) is the old sequence; current AHA adult CPR starts with compressions (C-A-B).
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse checks are limited to no more than 10 seconds before starting CPR, not up to 30 seconds.

prompt: A CPR feedback device shows a rescuer compressing an adult at 90 per minute. What rate should the rescuer aim for?

options.text: 80 to 100 per minute
90 to 110 per minute
100 to 120 per minute
120 to 140 per minute

explanation: AHA high-quality CPR uses 100–120 compressions per minute for adults, children and infants, with full recoil and minimal pauses.

distractorExplanations.a: 80–100 per minute is below the AHA target and lowers blood flow during CPR.
distractorExplanations.b: Rates under 100 reduce perfusion; the lower limit of the target range is 100 per minute.
distractorExplanations.d: Rates above 120 shorten refill time and usually reduce compression depth.

options.text: 1 inch (2.5 cm), not exceeding about 1.5 inches (4 cm)
1.5 inches (4 cm), not exceeding about 2 inches (5 cm)
2 inches (5 cm), not exceeding about 2.4 inches (6 cm)
3 inches (7.5 cm), not exceeding about 3.5 inches (9 cm)

explanation: Adequate depth is a key high-quality CPR metric; excessive depth can cause injury.

distractorExplanations.b: About 1.5 inches (4 cm) is the infant depth target; adults need at least 2 inches (5 cm).

prompt: Allowing complete chest recoil means:

options.text: Keeping light pressure on the sternum between compressions
Lifting the hands fully off the chest after each compression
Pausing about 2 seconds after each compression so the chest refills
Letting the chest return to normal position between compressions

distractorExplanations.b: Hands stay in contact with the chest; lifting off risks losing hand position and bouncing.
distractorExplanations.c: Recoil happens within each compression cycle at 100-120/min; deliberate pauses drop the rate.

About 30 seconds

options.text: 30:2 only

prompt: Infant chest compressions should be performed with which technique?

options.text: Two fingers on the sternum just below the nipple line
The heel of 1 hand, or 2 thumbs encircling the chest

Two fingers pressing on the xiphoid process

explanation: The 2025 AHA/AAP pediatric BLS guidelines dropped 2-finger compressions because they rarely reach adequate depth. distractorExplanations.b: A pulseless child needs compressions and early defibrillation.
distractorExplanations.c: Back blows are for a choking infant, not a witnessed collapse.

prompt: A child has a pulse above 60 but is not breathing. How often should rescue breaths be given?

options.text: 1 breath every second
1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds
1 breath every 6 seconds
2 breaths every 30 seconds, then a pulse check

explanation: Pediatric rescue breathing is 1 breath every 2–3 seconds (20–30 per minute), each with visible chest rise. Recheck the pulse about every 2 minutes.

distractorExplanations.a: Breathing this fast overinflates the lungs and causes gastric inflation.
distractorExplanations.c: Every 6 seconds is the adult rescue breathing rate.
distractorExplanations.d: That rate gives far too little ventilation for a child.

prompt: Where may a BLS provider check the pulse of an unresponsive 5-year-old?

options.text: Temporal artery at the side of the head
Radial artery only
Brachial artery only
Carotid or femoral artery

explanation: In children, check the carotid or femoral pulse for no more than 10 seconds. Infants use the brachial pulse and adults the carotid.

distractorExplanations.a: The temporal pulse is not used for BLS pulse checks.
distractorExplanations.b: The radial pulse may be weak or absent in shock and is not the BLS site.
distractorExplanations.c: The brachial pulse is the infant site; in children use the carotid or femoral.

prompt: An infant in cardiac arrest needs defibrillation. What is the order of preference for equipment?

options.text: No defibrillation at all, because infants should never be shocked
Adult AED first, since it is the fastest to use
Manual defibrillator, then AED with attenuator, then adult AED
AED with attenuator only; a manual defibrillator is not used

explanation: For infants, a manual defibrillator is preferred. If none is available, use an AED with a pediatric dose attenuator, and if neither is available, an AED without one.

distractorExplanations.a: Infants with shockable rhythms do need defibrillation.
distractorExplanations.b: An adult AED without attenuation is the last choice, used only when nothing else is available.
distractorExplanations.d: A manual defibrillator is preferred for infants when trained providers have one.

prompt: For which children should pediatric AED pads or a dose attenuator be used when available?

options.text: Children under 1 year only
Children under 12 years
Anyone under 18 years
Children under 8 years

explanation: Use pediatric pads or an attenuator for infants and children under 8 years (about 25 kg). Children 8 and older use adult pads and settings.

distractorExplanations.a: Infants qualify, but so do children up to about 8 years.
distractorExplanations.b: From age 8, adult pads and energy are used.
distractorExplanations.c: Adolescents and older children use adult pads.

prompt: How should a rescuer give breaths to an infant without a barrier device?

options.text: Give quick puffs from a few inches away
Breathe into the nose only, holding the mouth closed
Pinch the nose and cover only the mouth
Mouth over the infant's mouth and nose

explanation: For infants, the rescuer's mouth covers both the mouth and nose. Give each breath over 1 second with just enough volume to make the chest rise.

distractorExplanations.a: Puffs without a seal do not ventilate the lungs.
distractorExplanations.b: Mouth-to-nose is an option, but covering both is preferred for infants.
distractorExplanations.c: Pinch-and-mouth is the adult method; an infant's face is small enough to cover both.

prompt: How should an infant's head be positioned to open the airway for rescue breaths?

options.text: Neutral 'sniffing' position
Tilted far back as for an adult
Turned fully to one side
Chin tucked down toward the chest

explanation: An infant's airway is soft and easily blocked by too much extension. Use a neutral sniffing position, sometimes with a thin towel under the shoulders.

distractorExplanations.b: Overextending an infant's neck can kink the soft airway.
distractorExplanations.c: A rotated head does not open the airway for breaths.
distractorExplanations.d: Flexing the neck toward the chest kinks and blocks the infant airway.

prompt: A rescuer is giving CPR to a 6-year-old. How should compressions be delivered?

options.text: Always with one hand to avoid chest injury
With two fingers on the sternum
With two thumbs encircling the chest
One or two hands, by the child's size

explanation: For children, use the heel of one hand or both hands as for an adult, whichever achieves a depth of about one-third of the chest (about 2 inches).

distractorExplanations.a: One hand is fine for small children, but larger children may need two hands for depth.
distractorExplanations.b: Two-finger compressions were removed even for infants and are far too weak for a child.
distractorExplanations.c: The thumb technique is for infants, not school-age children.

prompt: How should a BLS provider check whether an infant is responsive?

options.text: Hold a mirror under the nose
Tap the foot and shout
Shake the infant by the shoulders
Pinch the earlobe hard

explanation: Tap the bottom of the infant's foot and shout to check responsiveness. Never shake an infant. If there is no response, call for help and check breathing and pulse.

distractorExplanations.a: A mirror test does not assess responsiveness and wastes time.
distractorExplanations.c: Shaking an infant can cause serious brain injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Painful stimuli are not the BLS method for infant responsiveness.

prompt: A child has a pulse of 50 per minute despite good rescue breathing. Which sign of poor perfusion means compressions should start?

options.text: A loud cry and active movement of all limbs
A respiratory rate of 20 per minute
Pink, warm skin and a strong central pulse
Cool, mottled skin, slow capillary refill

explanation: If a child's heart rate is below 60 with signs of poor perfusion, such as pallor, mottling, cool skin or delayed capillary refill, despite oxygenation and ventilation, start CPR.

distractorExplanations.a: A crying, moving child is perfusing and breathing.
distractorExplanations.b: Normal breathing does not by itself indicate poor perfusion.
distractorExplanations.c: Warm pink skin shows adequate perfusion, so compressions are not indicated.

prompt: In AHA BLS, which age group does 'infant' refer to?

options.text: Under 6 months only
Under 2 years of age
Newborns in the delivery room only
Under 1 year, excluding newborns

explanation: AHA BLS infant guidelines apply to babies under 1 year, excluding newly born infants at delivery, who follow neonatal resuscitation guidelines.

distractorExplanations.a: Infants include all babies under 1 year.
distractorExplanations.b: Infant guidelines stop at age 1; children use child guidelines.
distractorExplanations.c: Newly born babies at delivery follow neonatal resuscitation guidelines.

prompt: A lone rescuer with a cell phone finds an unresponsive infant who is not breathing, with no witnessed collapse. What should the rescuer do?

options.text: Carry the infant to the car and drive to a hospital
Hang up after calling and leave to find an AED first
Call EMS on speaker and start CPR right away
Do 2 minutes of CPR before using the phone

explanation: With a mobile phone, the lone rescuer calls EMS on speakerphone and starts CPR at once. If no AED has arrived after about 2 minutes, go get one if still alone.

distractorExplanations.a: Driving the infant yourself delays CPR and the arrival of EMS care.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving the infant delays CPR; with a phone, call on speaker and begin CPR.
distractorExplanations.d: With a phone at hand, there is no need to delay the call.

prompt: A lone rescuer is giving CPR to a 5-year-old without an advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio is used?
explanation: A single rescuer uses 30:2 for adults, children and infants. Two rescuers switch to 15:2 for children and infants.

distractorExplanations.b: 15:2 is used when two rescuers perform child CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: 5:1 is an outdated ratio no longer taught.
distractorExplanations.d: No AHA BLS ratio uses 15:1; children get 30:2 alone or 15:2 with two rescuers.

prompt: A child is receiving rescue breaths with a pulse present. How often should the rescuer recheck the pulse?

options.text: Every 10 seconds
Every 30 seconds or so
About every 2 minutes
Every 10 minutes

explanation: During rescue breathing, recheck the pulse about every 2 minutes, for no more than 10 seconds. Start compressions if the pulse is absent or below 60 with poor perfusion.

distractorExplanations.a: Checks this frequent interrupt ventilation and give no useful information.
distractorExplanations.b: Checking twice a minute is more often than needed and interrupts breaths.
distractorExplanations.d: Ten minutes is too long; a slowing heart rate must be caught early.

prompt: A 4-year-old is choking, cannot cough or speak, and is still responsive. Under 2025 AHA guidelines, what should the rescuer do?

options.text: Do a blind finger sweep to pull out the object
Give abdominal thrusts only until the object comes out
Give 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts, as for an infant
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts

explanation: For a responsive child with severe airway obstruction, 2025 AHA guidelines use repeated cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or the child becomes unresponsive.

distractorExplanations.a: Blind sweeps can push the object deeper.
distractorExplanations.b: The 2025 guidelines add back blows before abdominal thrusts for children.
distractorExplanations.c: Chest thrusts are the infant method; children get abdominal thrusts.

prompt: Where should the rescuer place the fist for abdominal thrusts on a choking adult?

options.text: Low on the abdomen just above the pubic bone
Thumb side in, just above the navel
Over the lower tip of the breastbone (xiphoid)
Over the center of the chest between the nipples

explanation: Make a fist and place the thumb side against the abdomen just above the navel and well below the breastbone, grasp it with the other hand and give quick inward-and-upward thrusts.

distractorExplanations.a: Too low a position does not push air up through the airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Thrusts on the xiphoid can injure the liver and other organs.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the chest-thrust position for pregnant or obese victims.

prompt: An adult starts choking while alone at home and cannot cough or speak. What can she do?

options.text: Lie down and wait for the object to pass on its own
Self abdominal thrusts or a chair-back thrust
Put a finger deep in her throat to sweep it out
Drink water to wash the object down

explanation: A choking person who is alone can give self abdominal thrusts with a fist or press the upper abdomen forcefully against a firm object such as a chair back or counter edge.

distractorExplanations.a: Lying down does not relieve severe obstruction and loss of consciousness may follow.
distractorExplanations.c: A blind sweep can push the object deeper.
distractorExplanations.d: Drinking can worsen the blockage and cause aspiration.

prompt: How should a rescuer hold a responsive choking infant to give back blows?

options.text: Held upside down by the ankles
Upright against the rescuer's shoulder
Face up on the forearm with the head higher than the chest
Face down on the forearm, head below the chest

explanation: Lay the infant face down along your forearm, resting on your thigh, with the head lower than the chest and the jaw supported. Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades.

distractorExplanations.a: Dangling an infant risks injury and gives no head or neck support.
distractorExplanations.b: Upright positioning does not let gravity help remove the object.
distractorExplanations.c: Face up is the position for chest thrusts, and the head should be lower.

prompt: How does a rescuer give back blows to a choking adult?

options.text: Lean them forward, strike between the shoulder blades
Strike the upper chest with an open palm
Tap gently on the neck below the head
Have the person lean back and strike the lower back hard

explanation: Support the chest with one hand, lean the person forward and give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the other hand, then give abdominal thrusts.

distractorExplanations.b: Chest strikes are not back blows and do not help dislodge the object.
distractorExplanations.c: Gentle neck taps do not generate enough force and risk injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaning back lets the object fall deeper, and the lower back is the wrong spot.

prompt: Which combination of signs most suggests opioid overdose?

options.text: Unresponsive, slow or no breathing, pinpoint pupils
Agitated, rapid breathing and widely dilated pupils
Facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech
Sweating, shaking and confusion with normal breathing

explanation: Opioid overdose typically causes unresponsiveness, slow or stopped breathing, pinpoint pupils and sometimes blue lips. Call EMS, support breathing and give naloxone.

distractorExplanations.b: These are more typical of stimulant toxicity or withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.c: Facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech are classic stroke signs, not overdose.
distractorExplanations.d: These fit low blood sugar more than opioid overdose.

prompt: A rescuer gave intranasal naloxone to a person with suspected opioid overdose, but there is no response after 2–3 minutes. What should happen next?

options.text: Stop and wait 30 minutes before trying again
Give a second dose from the same used spray device
Repeat with a new device in the other nostril
Assume it is not an opioid and stop all care

explanation: If there is no response, give a repeat dose every 2–3 minutes with a new device, alternating nostrils, while supporting breathing and continuing CPR if needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting leaves the person hypoxic; repeat doses are given every 2–3 minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Nasal devices are single-dose; a new device is needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Potent opioids may need several doses, and breathing support must continue.

prompt: After naloxone, a person with an opioid overdose is now breathing normally but is still drowsy. What should the rescuer do while waiting for EMS?

options.text: Give them strong coffee to keep them alert
Recovery position, and stay with them
Let them walk around the room to stay awake
Leave once their breathing is back to normal

explanation: Place a breathing but drowsy person in the recovery position to protect the airway, keep monitoring breathing and stay until EMS arrives, since re-sedation is possible.

distractorExplanations.a: Oral intake risks aspiration in a drowsy person.
distractorExplanations.c: Walking risks falls, and they may lose consciousness again.
distractorExplanations.d: Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so they need continued monitoring.

prompt: A rescuer is not sure whether an unresponsive person with slow breathing took opioids. Should naloxone be given?

options.text: Only after a blood test confirms opioids
Only if the person is under 18
Yes; it is unlikely to cause harm if no opioid is present
No; naloxone is dangerous unless opioid use is fully confirmed

explanation: Naloxone is safe to give when opioid overdose is suspected; it has little effect if no opioid is present. Give it while supporting breathing and calling EMS.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for confirmation delays a life-saving treatment.
distractorExplanations.b: Age does not determine whether naloxone is appropriate.
distractorExplanations.d: Naloxone has few effects in people without opioids in their system.

prompt: A restaurant patron's choking is relieved with abdominal thrusts, and he says he feels fine. What should the rescuer advise?

options.text: He should be checked by a medical provider
No follow-up is needed once he can talk
He should finish his meal to settle his stomach
He should lie down for an hour at the restaurant

explanation: Anyone who received abdominal thrusts should be evaluated by a healthcare provider, since thrusts can injure internal organs.

distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal thrusts can cause internal injuries that are not obvious right away.
distractorExplanations.c: Eating right away is unwise until he has been checked.
distractorExplanations.d: Rest alone does not rule out injury from the thrusts.

prompt: An adult clutches her throat and cannot speak. What should the rescuer do first?

options.text: Wait to see if she starts coughing on her own
Give her water to help her swallow
Start CPR right away while she is still standing
Ask if she is choking, then start back blows

explanation: The universal choking sign with no speech means severe obstruction. Confirm by asking, then give cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts.

distractorExplanations.a: Severe obstruction will not clear without help.
distractorExplanations.b: Drinking can worsen the obstruction and cause aspiration.
distractorExplanations.c: CPR is for an unresponsive person; she is still conscious.

prompt: After naloxone, a person wakes up, becomes agitated and starts vomiting. What should the rescuer do?

options.text: Hold them flat on their back so that they stay still
Turn them onto their side to keep the airway clear
Leave them alone until they calm down
Give a second naloxone dose to stop the vomiting

explanation: Withdrawal symptoms such as agitation and vomiting can follow naloxone. Turn the person on their side to protect the airway, stay calm and continue to monitor until EMS arrives.

distractorExplanations.a: Lying flat while vomiting risks aspiration.
distractorExplanations.c: They need monitoring for airway problems and re-sedation.
distractorExplanations.d: More naloxone will not stop vomiting and may worsen withdrawal.

prompt: A rescuer is much taller than a choking 3-year-old who is standing. How should the rescuer give abdominal thrusts?

options.text: Give the thrusts while standing upright
Kneel behind the child to reach the correct position
Lift the child off the ground and thrust in the air
Use chest thrusts instead because the child is small

explanation: Kneel or crouch behind a small child so your arms reach around at the right height. Give back blows and abdominal thrusts as for an adult, with less force.

distractorExplanations.a: Standing puts the hands in the wrong position on a small child.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifting makes thrusts harder to control and risks dropping the child.
distractorExplanations.d: Children get back blows and abdominal thrusts; chest thrusts are for infants.

prompt: An unresponsive infant who was choking now has a small object clearly visible in the mouth. What should the rescuer do?

options.text: Turn the infant upside down and shake
Remove the visible object, then continue CPR
Leave it in place and give breaths over it
Do a blind finger sweep deeper in the throat

explanation: During CPR for an unresponsive choking victim, look in the mouth before breaths. Remove an object only if you can see it, then continue CPR.

distractorExplanations.a: Shaking an infant can cause brain injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Breaths can push the object back down the airway.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind sweeps can lodge objects deeper; remove only what you can see.

prompt: A choking adult had a strong cough a moment ago, but now the cough is weak and silent and her lips are turning blue. What should the rescuer do?

options.text: Begin chest compressions while she stands
Keep encouraging her to cough
Start back blows and abdominal thrusts
Give her small sips of water

explanation: When mild obstruction becomes severe (weak or silent cough, inability to speak, cyanosis), start cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts.

distractorExplanations.a: Compressions are for an unresponsive victim.
distractorExplanations.b: A weak, silent cough means severe obstruction that coughing will not clear.
distractorExplanations.d: Drinking can worsen the obstruction and cause aspiration.

prompt: An adult collapses after touching a downed power line and is still in contact with it. What should the rescuer do first?

options.text: Pull the victim away with bare hands right away
Make sure the power is off before touching
Start CPR while the victim is still touching the line
Throw water on the victim to cool any burns

explanation: Scene safety comes first. Do not touch a victim in contact with electricity until the power source is turned off. Then assess and start CPR if needed.

distractorExplanations.a: The current can pass to the rescuer and injure or kill them.
distractorExplanations.c: Touching the victim while energized endangers the rescuer.
distractorExplanations.d: Water conducts electricity and increases the danger.

prompt: A child is pulled from a pool, unresponsive and not breathing. What should BLS rescuers emphasize?

options.text: Compression-only CPR to avoid giving breaths
Turn the child upside down to drain the lungs first
Wait for EMS because drowning victims cannot be resuscitated
High-quality CPR with early, effective rescue breaths

explanation: Drowning causes cardiac arrest from lack of oxygen, so ventilation is a priority. Start CPR with effective rescue breaths as soon as the victim is safely out of the water.

distractorExplanations.a: Drowning causes hypoxic arrest, so breaths are especially important.
distractorExplanations.b: Trying to drain water delays CPR and is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.c: Many drowning victims can be revived with prompt CPR.

prompt: Partway through a resuscitation, the team leader says, 'We have done 6 minutes of CPR, given 2 shocks, and the airway is secure. What else should we consider?' Which team element is this?

options.text: Knowing one's limitations
Constructive intervention
Summarize and reevaluate
Closed-loop communication

explanation: Periodic summarizing and reevaluating keeps the team aligned on what has been done and what to try next, and invites input from members.

distractorExplanations.a: That refers to asking for help when a task is beyond one's skills.
distractorExplanations.b: Constructive intervention is speaking up about an error.
distractorExplanations.d: Closed loop is confirming each order; this is a review of the whole situation.

prompt: During a resuscitation, a team member snaps at another for being slow. Which team element is being ignored?

options.text: Closed-loop communication
Knowledge sharing
Clear roles
Mutual respect

explanation: Mutual respect means calm, friendly, professional communication. Hostility increases stress and errors during a resuscitation.

distractorExplanations.a: Closed loop concerns confirming orders, not tone.
distractorExplanations.b: Knowledge sharing is about pooling information to solve problems.
distractorExplanations.c: Roles may be clear; the problem is the hostile tone.

prompt: A team leader assigns a member to manage the bag-mask, but she has never used one. What should she do?

options.text: Say so and ask for help or another task
Refuse to help with the resuscitation at all
Try it quietly and hope it works
Ask a family member to do it instead

explanation: Knowing one's limitations means telling the leader when a task is beyond your skills, so the leader can reassign it or provide help early.

distractorExplanations.b: She can still help with a task within her skills.
distractorExplanations.c: Hiding a lack of skill risks poor ventilation for the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Family members are not trained team members.

prompt: After a resuscitation ends, the team meets to review what happened. What is the main purpose of this debriefing?

options.text: Decide which team member should be disciplined
Complete billing documentation
Tell the family the details
Learn what went well and what to fix

explanation: Debriefing after a resuscitation helps teams learn: what went well, what did not, and how to improve CPR quality and teamwork next time.

distractorExplanations.a: Debriefings are learning-focused, not punitive.
distractorExplanations.b: Billing is separate from clinical debriefing.
distractorExplanations.c: Family communication is a separate step led by the appropriate provider.

prompt: Which resuscitation team role tracks the time of interventions and announces when rhythm checks are due?

options.text: Airway manager
AED operator
Compressor
Timer/recorder

explanation: The timer/recorder documents times of interventions and medications and announces when the next rhythm check or compressor switch is due.

distractorExplanations.a: The airway manager opens the airway and gives ventilations, not timekeeping.
distractorExplanations.b: The AED operator attaches the pads and runs the device.
distractorExplanations.c: The compressor focuses on high-quality compressions.

prompt: Family members show the BLS team a valid out-of-hospital DNR order for an elderly patient in cardiac arrest. What should the team do?

options.text: Ignore the form because only hospitals can use DNRs
Verify the form and withhold CPR per local protocol
Do CPR without using the AED
Start CPR anyway until a physician arrives

explanation: Follow local protocols: confirm the out-of-hospital DNR or POLST is valid, then withhold resuscitation. Continue supportive care and contact medical direction as required.

distractorExplanations.a: Out-of-hospital DNR or POLST forms are valid in many states.
distractorExplanations.c: A DNR applies to resuscitation as a whole, not just the AED.
distractorExplanations.d: A valid DNR means CPR should not be started if local rules are met.

prompt: Which finding means BLS rescuers should not start CPR?

options.text: Fixed and dilated pupils in both eyes
No pulse for 2 minutes
Rigor mortis with dependent lividity
A body temperature that feels cool

explanation: Obvious signs of irreversible death, such as rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decapitation or decomposition, mean CPR is not started. Otherwise begin CPR.

distractorExplanations.a: Pupils can be dilated during arrest and are not a reason to withhold CPR.
distractorExplanations.b: Pulselessness is the reason to start CPR.
distractorExplanations.d: Cool skin alone is not a sign of irreversible death.

prompt: A rescuer uses the E-C clamp technique with a bag-mask device. What do the 'C' and 'E' refer to?

options.text: C is compressions and E is exhalation
C is the cheek seal and E is the eye protection
C is the chin lift and E is the extension of the neck
Thumb and index finger make a C; other fingers an E

explanation: In the E-C clamp, the thumb and index finger form a C pressing the mask to the face, while the remaining three fingers form an E lifting the jaw into the mask.

distractorExplanations.a: E-C refers to hand position, not CPR phases.
distractorExplanations.b: The mask does not cover the eyes; the letters describe hand shape.
distractorExplanations.c: The letters describe hand shapes on the mask and jaw.

prompt: A man collapses in the middle of a busy street. What should the rescuer do before starting CPR?

options.text: Make the scene safe; move him only if needed
Start CPR right where he is, ignoring traffic
Wait for police before going near the victim
Drag him far away from the road before checking him

explanation: Scene safety comes first. Move the victim only if needed to protect rescuer and victim, then assess and begin CPR.

distractorExplanations.b: Ignoring traffic endangers both the rescuer and the victim.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting delays CPR; make the scene safe yourself if possible.
distractorExplanations.d: Move him only as far as needed for safety, then start CPR.

prompt: During a resuscitation, which communication style best supports the team?

options.text: Several people giving orders at the same time
Clear, concise messages in a calm voice
Long explanations so everyone understands the reasoning
Talking quietly to avoid alarming bystanders

explanation: Clear messages are concise and spoken in a calm, direct tone, which helps team members hear and act correctly.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiple leaders cause confusion; one leader gives orders.
distractorExplanations.c: Long explanations distract the team from tasks.
distractorExplanations.d: Quiet speech may not be heard over the noise.

prompt: The hospital code team arrives to take over from BLS rescuers. What should the rescuers provide?

options.text: Stop CPR and wait for the team to ask questions
A brief handoff: events, CPR time, shocks
A full medical history before the team starts work
Nothing; the code team will figure it out

explanation: Give a concise handoff, including what happened, when CPR started, shocks delivered and medications given, while compressions continue.

distractorExplanations.a: Compressions continue during the handoff.
distractorExplanations.c: Handoffs are brief so care continues without delay.
distractorExplanations.d: Important details like shock count and timing guide next steps.

prompt: The AED prompts 'Check pads' during use. What should the rescuer do?

options.text: Remove the pads and continue CPR without the AED
Press pads firmly or replace them
Turn off the AED and restart it
Ignore the prompt and keep compressing

explanation: A 'check pads' prompt means poor contact. Press the pads firmly, dry the skin or remove hair if needed, or replace the pads.

distractorExplanations.a: The AED is needed; fix the pad contact instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Restarting wastes time and does not fix poor contact.
distractorExplanations.d: Poor pad contact prevents analysis and shock.

prompt: A CPR coach watching a feedback monitor sees that compressions on an adult are only about 1.5 inches deep. What should the coach tell the compressor?

options.text: Good; 1.5 inches is the adult target
Stop so someone can check the pulse
Push harder, to at least 2 inches
Push faster, to about 140 per minute

explanation: Adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) but no more than 2.4 inches (6 cm) deep. A CPR coach gives specific, real-time feedback on depth, rate and recoil.

distractorExplanations.a: About 1.5 inches is the infant target; adults need at least 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.b: Pausing for a pulse check cuts compressions without fixing the depth.
distractorExplanations.d: Rates above 120 reduce depth further; the problem here is depth, not rate.
